## Understanding the problem

A taxi drives from point 1 to point n and never turns back. Each ride [start, end, tip] pays end − start + tip dollars, only one passenger may be carried at a time, and drop-off and pick-up may share a point. We choose a set of rides whose intervals are compatible (non-overlapping interiors) to maximize total money — textbook weighted interval scheduling along a line.

Example walkthrough: n = 5, rides = [[2,5,4],[1,5,1]] — taking ride [2,5,4] earns 5 − 2 + 4 = 7; chaining both rides is impossible (they overlap), so the answer is 7. For n = 20, picking [3,10,2] (9 dollars), [10,12,3] (5), and [13,18,1] (6) yields 20, beating alternatives such as including [11,12,2].

Constraints: n up to 10^5 and up to 3·10^4 rides. Earnings fit comfortably in 64-bit but can exceed 32-bit (3·10^4 rides × ~2·10^5 dollars ≈ 6·10^9), so C++/Java need long/long long.
k: A ride is worth end − start + tip regardless of context, so this is weighted interval scheduling on a line.
The forward-only drive makes position-based DP valid: best earnings at point p derive from dp[p−1] plus any ride ending exactly at p.
Use 64-bit accumulators — the maximum total exceeds the 32-bit range.

a.n: Approach 1: Sort by endpoint and scan back (quadratic DP)
a.i: Sort rides by end point. Let dp[i] be the best money using only the first i rides: either skip ride i (dp[i−1]) or take it, collecting gain = end − start + tip plus the best dp value among rides finishing no later than start_i, located with a backward scan through the sorted array. Simple and clearly correct, though the backward scans can cost quadratic time overall.
s: dp[0] = 0; for i = 1..m compute gain of ride i−1.
Scan j backwards from i−1 while rides[j−1] ends after start_i to find how many earlier rides are compatible.
Set dp[i] = max(dp[i−1], gain + dp[j]); answer dp[m].
a.t: O(m log m + m^2) — sorting plus backward compatibility scans per ride

a.n: Approach 2: Bucket rides by endpoint and sweep points (optimal)
a.i: Group rides by their end point and sweep p from 1 to n. At each p the driver either drives empty past it (dp[p] = dp[p−1]) or completes some ride ending at p: dp[start] + p − start + tip. Because ends bucket the transitions, every ride is examined exactly once and no binary search is needed; chaining at identical points works automatically since dp[start] already includes anything finished at start.
s: Create buckets endAt[p] holding (start, tip) for every ride ending at p.
For each (start, tip) in endAt[p]: dp[p] = max(dp[p], dp[start] + p − start + tip).
a.t: O(n + m) — one sweep over points; each ride contributes exactly one transition
a.sp: O(n + m) — buckets plus the dp array

## Wrap-up

Frame the task as weighted interval scheduling, show the sort-and-scan DP to establish recurrence, then optimize to the bucket sweep — interviewers like seeing both. Pitfalls: forgetting the tip (earnings are distance plus tip, not just tip); using int in C++/Java and overflowing; disallowing pickup at the exact drop-off point — the statement explicitly allows it, and using dp[start] (rather than dp[start−1]) is precisely what enables legal back-to-back chains; overlapping rides silently combined. Edge cases: a single ride, many rides sharing endpoints, rides covering point 1 or n. Follow-ups: maximize number of rides subject to minimum profit, handle multiple taxis, or process rides online as they arrive.
